newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - No end to Blair honeymoon in sight.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - No end to Blair honeymoon in sight.

text.p: Three months on from the general election, British Prime Minister Tony Blair is still merrily riding the tide of goodwill that swept his Labour party to power after 18 years of Conservative rule.
A by-election defeat in west London last week, though no great surprise, pricked Blair's bubble of invincibility.
But it failed to change the overall picture of a decisive, energetic start that has earned Labour record approval ratings and rave end-of-term reviews even from long-term critics.
"Labour's honeymoon has been extraordinary," Simon Heffer, praising the "ruthlessly brilliant discipline with which he runs his own party", wrote of Blair in the arch-Conservative Daily Mail.
Buoyed by a huge parliamentary majority and a party hungry to govern, Blair has wasted no time in making his mark.

Parliaments are being set up in Scotland and Wales. London is to have a powerful elected mayor. The Bank of England has been handed power over interest rates. Britain's schools are being shaken up, students will have to pay fees for the first time, and a root-and-branch reform of pensions is under way.

By itself, each of these measures will have a big impact on everyday life. Taken together, they lay the foundations of a radical programme of government that Blair hopes will stretch well into the new millennium.

"We have never had a Labour government elected for a full two terms, and our task must be to govern for the long term so that when the next election comes, the people of this country trust us and want to re-elect us with a continuing mandate," Blair said in a pep-talk to his members of parliament.

A MORI poll on July 31, the day parliament started a three-month holiday, gave 57 percent support for Labour, 34 points ahead of the Conservatives. At the election, 43.2 percent of the voters chose Labour.
CONTRAST WITH DIVIDED CONSERVATIVES

One reason why voters seem so impressed is that Labour's whirl of activity contrasts with the fallow final Conservative years when Blair's predecessor, John Major, was handicapped by deep splits in his party and a dwindling majority in parliament.
The Conservatives still seem dazed by their rout and, with new leader William Hague concentrating on internal party reforms, opposition in parliament has been largely ineffectual.

"Seldom in modern times has an opposition seemed so woefully irrelevant. The contrast with Tony Blair's energetic new administration could hardly be more glaring," the Daily Mail commented in an editorial.

Of all Blair's initiatives, none may prove to be more significant than his overtures to the Liberal Democrats, Britain's third party, which in many areas is now to the left of the "radically centrist" Labour.
Blair promised a new, inclusive politics and has kept his word by inviting Lib Dem leaders to join a consultative cabinet committee to discuss issues of mutual interest.
The eventual prize for Lib Dem leader Paddy Ashdown could be the introduction of proportional representation, which would give his party many more seats in the House of Commons.
The eventual prize for Blair could be a realignmnent of British politics that would entrench the centre-left in power and reduce the Conservatives to a marginalised rump.

Tony Wright, an influential Blairite MP, freely acknowledged what was at stake. "We're interested in keeping it in power for a generation and making the centre-left the dominant power in British politics," he said.
OTHER CHANGES

Blair has not stopped there. He has turned to prominent businessmen to serve as ministers or advisers and raised eyebrows by naming a flamboyant former Conservative minister, David Mellor, to head a task force on soccer.

At the same time, he has kept his distance from the trade unions, who founded Labour a century ago and still provide the lion's share of its funding, and cut Labour's national executive committee and annual conference -- sources of rivalry to past Labour governments -- down to size.
"Tony Blair is fast creating a new political party -- distinct in ideology and organisation from 'old' Labour," Peter Riddell commented in The Times. "No one should be surprised."
Blair has little patience with those voices of old Labour, led by former ministers Tony Benn and Roy Hattersley, who protest that he is ripping the guts out of the party.
But grassroots unease at the pace of modernisation is still likely to dominate Labour's annual conference in early October. Dozens of hostile motions have been submitted for debate.

Economic difficulties could also bring Blair's honeymoon to an end. He has blamed the three interest rate increases since he came to power on the failure of Major's administration to act promptly to curb inflation.

But finance minister Gordon Brown has been criticised for not doing enough to curb consumer spending, and the tough spending limits to which the government has shackled itself threaten strains before long in cash-strapped public services.

"We have a long way to go, and many trials to face in the future. But we have undoubtedly made a good beginning, and I hope that after a holiday we can all return to our desks to show the same vigour and commitment that we have displayed in our first few weeks in office," Blair told his ministers last week.
